nameStory: The doctorfish gets its name from the razor-sharp spines on either side of its tail, which resemble a surgeon's scalpel. These 'scalpels' can slice through skin if you're not careful handling this fish, earning it the medical nickname. All members of the surgeonfish family share this distinctive feature and the associated medical-themed names.
description: The doctorfish is a tropical surgeonfish that's extremely rare in New England waters, with only one recorded observation. This oval-shaped fish has a compressed, disc-like body typical of reef dwellers, with distinctive sharp spines near its tail. In its native warm waters, doctorfish typically grow to about 10-12 inches long and display muted brown to grayish coloring with subtle vertical bars.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Highly compressed, oval body that's taller than it is thick, like a dinner plate turned sideways - feels firm and muscular when handled

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Sharp, retractable spine on each side of the tail base that feels like a razor blade - handle with extreme caution as it can cause deep cuts

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dusky brown to gray overall with faint darker vertical bars running down the sides, and a subtle blue edge on the dorsal and anal fins

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Small, terminal mouth (at the front tip of the head) with tiny teeth designed for scraping algae - looks almost beak-like

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized fish reaching about 10-12 inches in length, with a deep body that makes it appear larger than its actual length

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Extremely out of place in New England - likely a stray from much warmer southern waters or an aquarium release

habitat: Doctorfish are not native to New England and are extremely rare visitors to our waters. The single recorded observation was likely either a fish carried far north by warm currents during an unusual weather pattern, or possibly an aquarium release. In their natural range, they inhabit coral reefs and rocky areas in tropical waters.

seasonality.spring: Any sighting would be extraordinary - if seen, likely to be lethargic from cold water temperatures that are far below their preferred range.
seasonality.summer: Most likely season for a rare sighting when water temperatures reach their warmest, though still far too cold for this tropical species to thrive.
seasonality.fall: Unlikely to survive cooling water temperatures if present, as these fish require consistently warm tropical conditions.
seasonality.winter: Virtually impossible to encounter as cold New England waters would be fatal to this tropical species.

funFact: Doctorfish can actually 'lock' their tail spines in an upright position when threatened, turning their tail into a medieval mace that can inflict serious wounds on predators - or unsuspecting anglers!
confusionNotes: In the extremely unlikely event you encounter one in New England, you might confuse it with other deep-bodied fish like black sea bass, but the doctorfish's distinctive tail spines and small scraping mouth make it unmistakable. Remember: if it has razor-sharp spines by the tail, you've found something very special and very far from home.
contextualKnowledge: Any doctorfish found in New England waters represents either an extraordinary natural occurrence or human intervention (aquarium release). These are quintessential tropical reef fish, and their presence here indicates either dramatic changes in ocean currents or irresponsible pet ownership practices.
compareHints: Since no other Acanthurus species occur in New England, compare this with other surgeonfishes if any are encountered. Doctorfish differ from related tangs by their more subdued coloration and specific pattern of faint vertical bars. Unlike the bright blues and yellows of many tropical tangs, doctorfish wear more camouflaged earth tones that help them blend with rocky reef backgrounds.
